items.title: How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love
items.description: “Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of her love letters to Susan an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a short and lovely poem, distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough. items.title: Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life
items.description: Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives. And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives. If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum. “Love quells fear,” Octavia Butler wrote in contemplating creativi

items.title: Legendary Cellist Pablo Casals, at Age 93, on Creative Vitality and How Working with Love Prolongs Your Life
items.description: "The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age."

items.title: The Art of Conversation: Timeless Do’s and Don’ts from 1866
items.description: "In disputes upon moral or scientific points, ever let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery."

items.title: Yes to Life, in Spite of Everything: Viktor Frankl’s Lost Lectures on Moving Beyond Optimism and Pessimism to Find the Deepest Source of Meaning
items.description: "Everything depends on the individual human being, regardless of how small a number of like-minded people there is... on each person... creatively making the meaning of life a reality in his or her own being."

items.title: How to Hear the Song of Life
items.description: “When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. Whoever has learned how to listen to trees no longer wants to be a tree. He wants to be nothing except what he is. That is home. items.title: Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter
items.description: Two of humanity's greatest minds explore the parallels between spacetime and psyche, the atomic nucleus and the self.

items.title: J.R.R. Tolkien on Fairy Tales, Language, the Psychology of Fantasy, and Why There’s No Such Thing as Writing “For Children”
items.description: "Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds."

items.title: Love Anyway
items.description: You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal. items.title: Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing
items.description: "Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time."

items.title: Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go
items.description: "We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go."

items.title: The Four Buddhist Mantras for Turning Fear into Love
items.description: "When you love someone, the best thing you can offer that person is your presence."

items.title: Loving vs. Being in Love: Jane Welsh Carlyle on Navigating the Heart’s Contradictions
items.description: "A passion, like the torrent in the violence of its course, might perhaps too, like the torrent, leave ruin and desolation behind... My love for you... is deep and calm, more like the quiet river, which refreshes and beautifies where it flows."

items.title: Where the Joy Is
items.description: One of the most important things I have learned about life is that joy is a choice, an orientation, a practice of bending the mind in the direction of gladness — a choice increasingly countercultural in our age of competitive complaint, and yet all the more urgent precisely because our world gives us so many valid reasons for despair. “Experience of conflict and a load of suffering has taught me that what matters above all is to celebrate joy… Life is wasted when we make it more terrifying, prec

items.title: Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age
items.description: "A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent."
